# Interactive

<span data-language-key="interactive"></span>

No install and no account. Each of these runs in your browser, in English or
Spanish, and answers a question the pages can only describe: move a control and
the shapes, the strides and the numbers move with it. Every one is also linked
from the section it belongs to, in the [handbook](./tensors_workshop_plan_with_quizzes.html)
and in the notebooks.

:::: {.widget-grid}
::: {.resource-card}
### 🧮 Broadcasting simulator

<span data-language-key="broadcasting-simulator"></span>

Type two shapes. Watch NumPy line them up from the right, pad the short one, and
stretch every axis of size 1 — or refuse, and say which axis. Section 03.

[Try shapes](interactive/broadcasting-simulator.html?lang=en){.resource-button}
:::

::: {.resource-card}
### 🧊 The image tensor

<span data-language-key="image-tensor"></span>

Three real photos as one 4-D tensor, a cube per byte, up to 128 × 128.
Transpose it and watch the cubes follow the new shape while not one byte of
the buffer moves; reshape it and watch the picture break; rewrite the buffer C, Fortran or channels_last and watch
only the memory move. Every click prints the NumPy and PyTorch that does it.
Section 04.

Straight to [transpose](interactive/image-tensor.html?lang=en#transpose),
[reshape](interactive/image-tensor.html?lang=en#reshape) or
[the memory layout](interactive/image-tensor.html?lang=en#memory).

[Open the image tensor](interactive/image-tensor.html?lang=en){.resource-button}
:::

::: {.resource-card}
### 👁️ Attention, from words to weights

<span data-language-key="attention-stage"></span>

One four-word sentence, "I know you know", followed through a single
attention head with every number small enough to add up by hand: the words
cut into tokens, the tokens coded as ids, the ids fetching rows of an
embedding table, those rows projected into queries, keys and values, the
scores, why they are divided by √d_k, softmax turning them into weights that
sum to one, and the weighted average that is the output. Then more heads,
and the batch a real model is handed. Every picture carries the NumPy that
computes it. Sections 04 and 06, and Appendix B.

Straight to [why √d_k](interactive/attention-stage.html?lang=en#scale),
[the scores](interactive/attention-stage.html?lang=en#scores),
[softmax](interactive/attention-stage.html?lang=en#softmax) or
[every head gets its own axis](interactive/attention-stage.html?lang=en#heads).

[Open the attention stage](interactive/attention-stage.html?lang=en){.resource-button}
:::

::: {.resource-card}
### 📐 Projection & SVD stage

<span data-language-key="projection-svd-stage"></span>

Least squares is a projection: scroll, and watch a target vector's shadow land
on the plane its predictors span, with the residual meeting it at a right
angle. Then the SVD portal, where a unit circle becomes an ellipse and
A v = σ u stops being notation, and on to the eigenvectors, two nearly
collinear columns and float32 dividing by exactly zero. One problem, sections
07, 08 and 09.

Straight to [the SVD portal](interactive/linalg-stage.html?lang=en#portal),
[the eigenvectors](interactive/linalg-stage.html?lang=en#eigen) or
[float32 dividing by zero](interactive/linalg-stage.html?lang=en#precision).

[Open the projection & SVD stage](interactive/linalg-stage.html?lang=en){.resource-button}
:::

::: {.resource-card}
### 🎙️ The audio tensor

<span data-language-key="voice-tensor-stage"></span>

Air becomes numbers: 48 000 a second, each rounded to 16 bits, written down as
an array you can listen to. Then one window is cut out of it, the transform is
asked which frequencies are in that window, and the window hops along to build
a frequency-by-time matrix, 513 × 465 — and you can hear what a transpose does
to it. It ends on the rank-4 batch a model is handed, three recordings stacked.
Sections 00, 02, 04 and 09, and Appendix E.

Straight to [one window](interactive/voice-stage.html?lang=en#frame),
[the transform](interactive/voice-stage.html?lang=en#spectrum),
[the best rank-k there is](interactive/voice-stage.html?lang=en#lowrank) or
[the batch](interactive/voice-stage.html?lang=en#batch).

[Open the audio tensor](interactive/voice-stage.html?lang=en){.resource-button}
:::
::: {.resource-card}
### 🚕 Tucker and CP

<span data-language-key="tucker-cp-stage"></span>

One real tensor, factorised two ways: 6,383 New York taxi trips, pickup borough
by dropoff borough by hour of day, as a cube of voxels you can turn and click —
three quarters of it one Manhattan route. Watch the cube lay itself flat into
each unfolding, see what the SVD of one finds, and reassemble a small core plus
three factor matrices: 480 numbers down to 102, at 6.7% error, one core entry
carrying 99% of the fit. Then build the best rank-1 term there is, see what
several of them look like, play alternating least squares one solve at a time
from five starts that do not all agree, and spend one parameter budget both
ways. Sections 10 and 11, and Appendix C.

Straight to [the cube laid flat](interactive/factor-stage.html?lang=en#unfold),
[the core and its three factors](interactive/factor-stage.html?lang=en#tucker),
[one rank-1 term](interactive/factor-stage.html?lang=en#rank1),
[ALS, solve by solve](interactive/factor-stage.html?lang=en#als) or
[the same budget spent two ways](interactive/factor-stage.html?lang=en#budget).

[Open Tucker and CP](interactive/factor-stage.html?lang=en){.resource-button}
:::
::: {.resource-card}
### 🧬 DNA to an edit

<span data-language-key="genome-stage"></span>

A gene is a string over a four-letter alphabet, which is already a tensor: 180
bases of a real cas12a gene become a 180 × 4 grid of ones and zeros, one 1 per
row. Follow that one stretch through everything a cell does with it. A sliding
window cuts 161 views out of it without copying a base. An enzyme reads one
strand and the RNA comes out reading like the other, because transcription is a
4 × 4 matrix and two complements undo each other. A codon is three one-hot
vectors multiplied together, the genetic code is a 4 × 4 × 4, and translation is
one contraction between them — where swapping a codon's third base is the
page's first edit, and often changes nothing. Sixty residues land on 18 points
of a property map; the whole protein, as AlphaFold predicts it, is a
`(1300, 3)` array whose distances are one broadcast; and checking a guide
against every window of the sequence is one einsum — 161 windows, one perfect
match, the runner-up at 12 of 20. Under every picture is the gene itself, with
the stretch that picture is looking at lit. It shows what the arithmetic is; it
is not a tool for designing anything. Sections 04 and 06, and Appendix G.

Straight to [transcription as a matrix](interactive/genome-stage.html?lang=en#transcribe),
[the genetic code as a 4 × 4 × 4](interactive/genome-stage.html?lang=en#codons),
[translation as one contraction](interactive/genome-stage.html?lang=en#translate),
[the fold and its grid of distances](interactive/genome-stage.html?lang=en#fold) or
[the search as one einsum](interactive/genome-stage.html?lang=en#search).

[Open DNA to an edit](interactive/genome-stage.html?lang=en){.resource-button}
:::
::: {.resource-card}
### ♟️ AlphaTensor: from a rule to a game

<span data-language-key="alphatensor-stage"></span>

Multiplying two 2 × 2 matrices takes eight multiplications, and eight looks
like a fact about the problem. It is not. Write the rule down as a list of its
eight products, put a 1 at each one, and the rule is a 4 × 4 × 4 block of zeros
and ones that multiplies matrices with one `einsum`. Split that block into
pieces that each cost one multiplication and you have an algorithm: add
Strassen's seven pieces one at a time and the count of wrong cells goes *up*,
from 8 to 12, before it falls to zero, because the pieces overshoot and cancel.
Run the seven on numbers, then on the quarters of a matrix, and one saved
multiplication becomes 73.7% of them at 1,024 × 1,024. Then turn it round:
start from the cube and subtract pieces until nothing is left. That is the
game AlphaTensor plays. A single move has 244,140,625 choices; of the 128,000
simplest, 8 look like progress and Strassen's is not one of them; and a player
who always takes the best-looking move finds eight, never seven. The last
picture is the record board, where 3 × 3 is still open between 19 and 23.
Under every picture is the cube laid flat, showing what that picture does to
it. The page plays the game; it does not run or train a network, and
AlphaTensor's own results are quoted from the paper. Sections 06 and 11, and
[deep dive 20](https://colab.research.google.com/github/project-delphi/tensors-workshop/blob/main/notebooks/20-alphatensor.ipynb).

Straight to [the rule as a cube](interactive/alphatensor-stage.html?lang=en#cube),
[the product as one einsum](interactive/alphatensor-stage.html?lang=en#read),
[Strassen's seven blocks](interactive/alphatensor-stage.html?lang=en#strassen),
[the game](interactive/alphatensor-stage.html?lang=en#game) or
[why greedy finds eight](interactive/alphatensor-stage.html?lang=en#greedy).

[Open AlphaTensor](interactive/alphatensor-stage.html?lang=en){.resource-button}
:::
